The dict layout itself is documented at the top of dictobject.c L28: a dense dk_indices table pointing into an ordered entries array, which is what makes those probes cache-friendly and keeps insertion order. That is the entire conceptual gap between “garbage” and “cycle garbage” — and it is why small ints, interned strings, and function defaults are cheap while huge interlinked object graphs cost collection time.

The GIL: One Lock to Rule the Loop

The GIL exists because the design above assumes exactly one thread is executing bytecode per interpreter at a time. Threads coordinate through take_gil, L286 and drop_gil, L217: a thread that has run for its switch interval sets the eval_breaker, the running loop notices it at the next periodic check, drops the lock, and a waiting thread wakes to take it. The shared state lives in struct _gil_runtime_state, passed straight into drop_gil_impl, L203, so the drop-request protocol is readable in a single screen of C. C-level releases happen around blocking I/O so that network threads never stall the interpreter — the mechanism behind everything from Flask request handling to FastAPI worker pools.

The tree already carries the no-GIL path. Python/gc_free_threading.c sits next to Python/gc.c, and ceval.c guards thread-local bytecode with Py_GIL_DISABLED conditionals. In a free-threaded build the per-object locking strategy changes, which is exactly why the immortal-reference encoding in refcount.h matters: it removes shared-counter writes for objects that can never be freed.

From Install to Your First Model

Building CPython from this tree is deliberately boring. On Linux and macOS the documented path in README.rst L53 is ./configure, make, make test, and sudo make install; a debug build passes --with-pydebug to configure as shown at README.rst L87. On Windows the entry point is the PCbuild solution, linked from README.rst L76. Passing --enable-optimizations to configure turns on profile-guided optimization before make (README.rst L94), and note that ceval.c contains MSVC-specific PGO pragmas precisely because the eval loop is the hottest function in the binary.

Once installed, your first model is a two-liner: pip install scikit-learn, then fit a LinearRegression on a few hundred rows. Every step of that fit — the Python loop over features, the dict lookups for attribute access, the calls into compiled BLAS code — runs through the exact chain in the diagrams above, from Py_BytesMain down to the eval loop handing off to C extensions when LangChain-style tools or ORM-heavy Django views call into NumPy-backed code.

Honest Limits

Everything cited here is a snapshot of main at commit 8c212aa0de53 — line numbers drift fast on this repo, so re-grep before quoting them elsewhere. The free-threading and JIT paths are build-time options, not defaults: whether Python/jit.c or Python/gc_free_threading.c is active depends entirely on the configure flags your binary was built with. The tier-2 optimizer interfaces (Python/optimizer.c, Python/optimizer_analysis.c) are still evolving, and the bytecode DSL in Python/bytecodes.c is regenerated rather than edited by hand — do not patch generated files. Finally, this tour follows one execution path; import machinery, async generators, and the C extension protocol are whole subsystems of their own, and the framework source tours of FastAPI and Flask only make sense once you know the interpreter they ride on.
entry.summary: A verified walk through CPython's main branch: tokenizer, PEG parser, bytecode compiler, the ceval dispatch loop, refcounting, the cycle collector, and the GIL.

entry.title: Inside Deno: How a Rust Core Hosts V8 and Guards Every Op

link.title: Inside Deno: How a Rust Core Hosts V8 and Guards Every Op

entry.content:
You write await fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/models") in TypeScript and a response comes back. But between that one line and the network card there is a boundary most JavaScript developers never see: the call leaves V8’s world of heap objects and hidden classes and enters a Rust program that owns the socket, the TLS state machine, and the event loop. What actually crosses that line? A small integer op id, a promise id, and a handful of marshalled arguments. Everything else — buffering, cancellation, timers — is Rust code waiting on a Tokio future that your JavaScript knows nothing about.

The second invisible mechanism is the permission prompt. When you run deno run --allow-net=api.github.com main.ts and the script touches another host, you get a terminal prompt asking for --allow-net=api.openai.com. That is not a runtime library wrapper or a monkey-patched fetch. It is a check executed inside the op implementation itself, in Rust, before the request is ever built: op_fetch in the fetch extension borrows PermissionsContainer from OpState and calls check_net_url(&url, "fetch()") at line 479 of ext/fetch/lib.rs. If you granted nothing, the prompt fires from the same code path. There is no way for user JavaScript to reach the socket without walking through that check, because there is no other door to the socket.

And why did Deno choose V8 plus Rust in the first place? Because the architecture is a classic embedder split, the same shape you see when CPython embeds native extensions or when Rust web servers like Actix Web park thousands of futures on a few threads. V8 executes JS and JITs it well; Rust owns everything V8 cannot do — sockets, files, crypto, process spawning — and a thin, generated bridge glues the two. The result is a runtime where every Web API is really an op registration plus a Rust function, and where the entire event loop is a Future polled from Tokio.

This post is a source tour of the denoland/deno repository, main branch, as of 2026-11-10. Every symbol, file, and line number below was verified against the actual tree with grep before publication — note that the core recently moved from a top-level core/ directory into libs/core/ and the op macro into libs/ops/, so older write-ups citing core/ops.rs are pointing at a layout that no longer exists.

The boot path from `cli/main.rs` down to `JsRuntime`, with the op bridge and permission boundary that every Web API call must cross. Generated from the verified denoland/deno source graph.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The binary’s main is deliberately trivial — main, L3 only calls deno::main(), so the real boot — panic hook, logging, fd limits, prompt callbacks, V8 platform init — lives in main, L859. The comment there explains that V8’s platform must be initialized on the parent thread of every isolate thread.
  • Startup speed comes from a snapshot, not from re-parsing JS at launch: CLI_SNAPSHOT, L4 embeds a precompiled V8 heap blob via include_bytes!, produced at build time by create_runtime_snapshot, L50 from all extension sources.
  • The user-facing handle is MainWorker, L194, constructed through bootstrap_from_options, L441 and a shared common_runtime, L1282 factory that fills a 20-field RuntimeOptions struct.
  • JsRuntime, L456 is the heart: one Rust struct owning one V8 isolate, its realms, allocations, and the module map. It exposes execute_script, mod_evaluate, and the event loop your program lives on.
  • Extensions are wired by lazy_init_extensions, L612, which passes per-extension args for web, fetch, cache, websocket, crypto, net, kv, ffi, http, io, fs, and os into the core registry — this is where Deno.fetch becomes real code.
  • Each realm carries its own op driver: the alias at OpDriverImpl, L64 resolves to FuturesUnorderedDriver, which parks in-flight async op futures until the event loop polls them.
  • The op boundary is generated code: the op2, L25 proc macro expands ordinary Rust functions into fast-call capable dispatchers, with each call receiving an OpCtx, L102 carrying the op id, declaration pointer, and shared state.
  • Permissions ride along as ordinary state: ops borrow PermissionsContainer, L4132 from OpState, so a network op cannot run without a check happening inside Rust.
  • Module loading is pluggable: CliModuleLoader, L1322 implements the core ModuleLoader, L61 trait, feeding the module graph, npm resolution, and load hooks into the isolate.

The detail view follows one fetch call and one module load end to end: extension registration, the op2-generated dispatcher, the FuturesUnordered op driver, the Rust-to-JS `__eventLoopTick` callback, and the permission prompter. Same verified source graph, one level deeper.

Two Layers, One Isolate

JsRuntime::new at new, L756 takes the RuntimeOptions the worker built — module loader, startup snapshot, extensions, inspector flag — and creates the V8 isolate. After construction, Rust reaches into JavaScript exactly once to wire callbacks: store_js_callbacks, L1703 grabs Deno.core.__eventLoopTick, __processTimers, and __drainNextTickAndMacrotasks from the global Deno object as v8::Function handles. Those three functions are the entire reverse channel: Rust will later call back into them to resolve promises and run timers.

The JS side of core lives in 01_core.js, where __eventLoopTick at L461 consumes (promiseId, isOk, res) triples and settles the matching promise. This is why Deno’s microtask ordering is explicit: op resolution defers microtask checkpoints, and Rust drives the drain separately. Meanwhile the bootstrap script bootstrapMainRuntime, L936 installs the Deno namespace, sets up globals, then deletes globalThis.bootstrap so embedder internals stop being reachable.

The event loop itself is honest about what it is: run_event_loop, L2321 is a poll_fn over poll_event_loop, L2390, and its doc comment promises it will not resolve while dynamic imports, pending ops, or inspector sessions remain. Your whole program is one future that Tokio polls until everything drains.

The Op Bridge: From JavaScript Call to Rust Future

Every Web API operation is declared as a Rust function annotated with #[op2], and the proc macro at op2, L25 generates the machinery: argument extraction from V8 fast API calling conventions, a slow fallback path, and for async ops a submit wrapper. The extension declaration in the fetch crate shows the pattern — deno_core::extension!, L159 lists op_fetch, op_fetch_send, op_fetch_custom_client, and friends plus eight lazy-loaded JS files that define the standard fetch() surface.

When an async op runs, map_async_op_infallible, L36 turns the Rust future into a driver submission. The OpDriver, L52 trait’s submit_op_infallible at L56 parks the future inside FuturesUnorderedDriver at FuturesUnorderedDriver, L56, keyed by promise id. Nothing in user JavaScript ever blocks: the op returns a promise immediately, and the driver’s results are batched back into __eventLoopTick when the event loop next polls.

Sync ops take the fast path: V8’s fast API calls let a compiled JS function invoke the Rust function directly without leaving machine code, which is why #[op2] exists at all. The macro decides per-op whether fast calls are legal based on the signature, falling back to the slow path when arguments get exotic. If you have read about how Node or Bun schedule their native bindings, this is the same shape — but here the binding layer is a generated Rust dispatcher, and it is shared by every extension from fetch to FFI.

Permissions Are Just Another Type in OpState

OpState at OpState, L395 is a typed bag: resources, timers, extension options, and the permission container all live there. An op that wants the network does state.borrow::<PermissionsContainer>() and checks. In the fetch op at op_fetch, L436, the scheme is inspected before the permission check — file: URLs route to a file fetch handler, and only http/https reach check_net_url, L4753 with the api name "fetch()" at L479. TCP is equally guarded: op_net_connect_tcp at op_net_connect_tcp, L589 calls check_net with the resolved host and port at L624.

The container itself wraps Permissions at L3689 behind an Arc<Mutex<...>>, with per-verb UnaryPermission types. The read check at check, L3225 audits and delegates to check_desc, and when nothing is granted the prompter is consulted: permission_prompt, L99 renders the TTY allow/deny prompt. Because checks happen inside op implementations, worker boundaries and child permissions funnel through the same container — there is exactly one place to audit.

Module Loading: From URL to V8 Module

The core defines what a loader must do — ModuleLoader, L61 with resolve and load — but the CLI owns the real implementation. CliModuleLoader::load at load, L1428 returns a ModuleLoadResponse and can delegate to JS load hooks asynchronously when they are registered; prepare_load at L1611 drives graph prefetch. Execution starts at execute_main_module, L989, which loads the entry module and then races module evaluation against the event loop in evaluate_module, L934 using tokio::select! with biased mode — the comment notes that bias matters for determinism.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one command per platform, straight from the repository README: curl -fsSL https://deno.land/install.sh | sh on Mac and Linux, irm https://deno.land/install.ps1 | iex on Windows, plus Homebrew, Chocolatey, WinGet, and Scoop variants. Building from source is a Rust toolchain exercise; the README points to the contributing guide’s “Building from source” section, and the workspace Cargo.toml shows the member crates you would compile — cli, ext/*, and libs/* including libs/core and libs/ops.

Your first program needs no package install at all. Create server.ts with Deno.serve((_req: Request) => new Response("Hello, world!")) and run deno run --allow-net server.ts — the README’s exact example, served at localhost:8000. The same zero-install property is what makes a first LLM call trivial: a script that does await fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/models") uses the exact op_fetch path described above, needing only --allow-net=api.openai.com. Compare that with the Node.js and Bun ecosystems where an HTTP client package usually arrives before line one — the capability you are granting is visible on the command line before the code runs.

Honest Limits

Three things worth knowing before you cite internals. First, the layout is in motion: core/ became libs/core/, the op macro became libs/ops/, and the permissions crate lives at runtime/permissions/ — any tutorial citing the old paths describes a tree that no longer exists on main, and line numbers in this post will drift the day after publish. Second, fast calls are an optimization, not a guarantee: the op2 macro ships both dispatch_fast.rs and dispatch_slow.rs, and ops with exotic signatures always take the slow path, so “zero-cost binding” is directionally true, not literally true. Third, the permission model guards access through ops, which is precisely why it is effective for files, network, and environment — but the fetch op checks the URL scheme before the net check, meaning file: fetches are permission-gated by the read permission path instead of net. Deno’s own code comments make these boundaries explicit; trust the source, not the marketing.
entry.summary: A source tour of denoland/deno showing how JsRuntime embeds V8, how the op2 bridge turns JavaScript calls into Rust futures, and where permission checks actually run.

entry.title: Inside the Go Runtime: How G/M/P, Channels, and the Tricolor GC Actually Run Your Code

link.title: Inside the Go Runtime: How G/M/P, Channels, and the Tricolor GC Actually Run Your Code

entry.content:
Every Go developer has felt the gap. You write go handler(conn) and the function starts running on a stack measured in kilobytes — tens of thousands of them per process, on the same machine where a Python program threads awkwardly around the GIL. In CPython, a thread is an OS thread with a lock around bytecode execution; in Go, concurrency is a runtime-internal illusion layered on top of a small number of real threads. That gap is not magic. It is roughly eight thousand lines of exacting Go code in src/runtime/proc.go, and understanding it changes how you write servers — the same discipline that powers gin, etcd, and kubernetes.

The pain shows up in production telemetry. Why does p99 latency jump right when a channel’s buffer fills and senders start parking? Why does the GC steal CPU from your hot handler even though the world is never fully stopped? Why does a goroutine blocked on a socket cost nothing, while one spinning in a tight loop is preempted exactly 10 milliseconds later? Each question has a precise answer in the runtime source — the scheduler’s spinning-thread protocol, the GC pacer’s assist mechanism, and one constant called forcePreemptNS.

This post tours the actual implementation. The target is the golang/go repository on GitHub, branch master, and every symbol, file, and line number cited below was grepped and verified against a real checkout of that tree — no invented identifiers, no stale blog-lore. Two diagrams map the territory: an overview of the execution path from go build to a running goroutine, and a detailed graph of the scheduler, channel, allocator, GC, netpoller, and stack machinery.

Overview of the Go execution path: the toolchain produces a binary whose entry point is the runtime, the runtime boots the G/M/P scheduler, and channel, allocation, and GC operations all funnel back into the same scheduling loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The binary starts in the runtime, not your code. CmdBuild, L29 drives the build, but the linked executable’s real entry point is runtime.main, L152, which first runs schedinit, L843 to bootstrap the allocator, GC, and the array of Ps.
  • go statements are allocations, not syscalls. newproc, L5341 creates a new g via newproc1 and hands it to runqput, L7550, which fills the P’s runnext slot; runqputslow, L7596 spills half the queue to the global one only when the 256-slot ring overflows.
  • Scheduling is P-first, then global, then theft. schedule, L4157 calls findRunnable, L3409, which tries the local queue, the global run queue via globrunqget, L7353, GC mark workers, and finally stealWork, L3848 — stealing half a victim P’s queue in one batch with runqgrab, L7734.
  • Blocking never blocks the thread. chansend, L168 hands its value straight to a parked receiver or buffers it; on a full buffer it enqueues a sudog and calls gopark, L456, and the same thread is instantly back in schedule looking for other work.
  • Allocation is almost lock-free. mallocgc, L1016 serves small objects from a per-P mcache; mcache.refill, L160 pulls a fresh span from the mheap.central, L211 lists only when the local span is exhausted.
  • The GC rides the scheduler instead of pausing it. gcStart, L733 flips the heap into _GCmark and enables the write barrier; gcBgMarkWorker, L1766 goroutines are handed to Ps by findRunnableGCWorker, so marking competes fairly with user goroutines rather than monopolizing cores.
  • Wakeups converge on the same queues. goready, L492 (backed by ready, L1122) is the single re-entry point: a finished syscall, a ready socket, or a completed channel send all end with a G dropped onto some P’s run queue.

The detailed graph follows one coherent execution path — spawn, schedule, block on a channel, allocate, trigger GC, and wake through the netpoller — with every node pinned to a verified line in the master tree.

Goroutines Are Not Threads: The G/M/P Machine

Three structs carry the whole design. g, L471 is a goroutine: stack bounds, a status field cycling through runnable, running, and waiting, and a saved register buffer. m, L615 is an OS thread with its own g0 scheduling stack. p, L774 is the crucial middle layer — a scheduler context owning a local run queue, an mcache, and timers. An M must hold a P to execute Go code; work therefore lands on a P first, and only contention pushes it global, onto schedt, L936.

The fairness machinery lives outside the scheduler loop entirely. sysmon, L6550 is a thread that runs without a P, waking between 20 microseconds and 10 milliseconds; its retake, L6694 pass does two jobs. If an M has been stuck in a syscall past a sysmon tick, the P is handed off via handoffp, L3141 to a fresh thread. If a goroutine has occupied the same P past forcePreemptNS — a 10-millisecond constant defined at proc.go, L6692 — preemptone, L6930 forces it out, which is why an untight loop can never starve its siblings. When a goroutine finally returns, goexit0, L4513 resets it to _Gdead and returns the thread to schedule; spawning an M (newm, proc.go, L2870) happens only when idle Ps actually need threads.

When a Channel Blocks: sudog, sendq, and gopark

A channel is a small struct, not a queue library. hchan, L34 holds a circular buffer with send and receive indexes, two waiter lists, and — remarkably — a single lock. The send path in chansend, L168 has three outcomes. First, if a receiver is already parked on recvq, send (chan.go, L310) copies the value directly into the receiver’s stack slot and marks it runnable — the buffered channel memory is bypassed entirely. Second, if buffer space exists, the value lands at sendx and the lock is released; the whole fast path costs one mutex acquire.

Only the third outcome blocks, and it does so without blocking the thread. The sender allocates a sudog, L404 — the runtime’s record of “one goroutine waiting on one channel” — via acquireSudog, L499, enqueues it on sendq at chan.go, L265, and calls gopark. The M is immediately free; when a receiver or closechan, L406 completes the operation, the parked G re-enters the normal queues. The mirror image lives in chanrecv, L516, where a waiting sender’s value is stolen via sendDirect (chan.go, L384). One subtlety: parkingOnChan and chanparkcommit, L741 exist so the stack-shrink machinery never moves a stack out from under a parked sudog.

The Allocator and the Stacks Beneath It

mallocgc is a size dispatcher. Tiny no-scan objects under 16 bytes go to mallocgcTiny, L1153, which packs several small strings into one 8-byte block; medium objects split between mallocgcSmallNoscan, L1309 and two scan-aware paths; anything large goes straight to mallocgcLarge, L1638 and the heap. The per-P mcache (mcache.go, L48) caches exactly one span per size class, and the class count is NumSizeClasses << 1 — scan and no-scan variants (mheap.go, L576). That is why allocation on a busy multi-core server rarely touches a shared lock: the P-local span absorbs it.

Goroutine stacks follow the same “pay for what you use” philosophy. A new G starts on a small stack from stackalloc, L344; on overflow, newstack, L1067 allocates a doubled stack and adjustframe, L701 rewrites every pointer in every frame during the copy. Oversized stacks are reclaimed at GC time by shrinkstack, L1298. This is why deeply recursive code can be as cheap in Go as iterative code — the runtime quietly moves your stack between the OS pages.

The Tricolor GC and Your p99

The collector is concurrent, tricolor mark-sweep with a hybrid write barrier. gcStart, L733 begins with a very short stop-the-world window that only switches the phase to _GCmark and enables the write barrier (mgc.go, L259); application goroutines resume immediately after. Marking itself is spread across per-P workers: gcBgMarkWorker, L1766 loops forever, and the scheduler hands workers out through findRunnableGCWorker (mgcpacer.go, L859) — GC work literally competes with your goroutines inside findRunnable, which is the design’s central trick.

The actual marking is a work-stealing traversal. gcDrain, L1253 pulls grey objects from a local gcWork buffer; markroot, L221 scans globals and every goroutine stack (scanstack, L904); scanblock, L1493 follows pointers and greyobject, L1653 shades discovered objects. If allocation outpaces the background workers, the mutator pays: gcAssistAlloc, L499 makes the allocating goroutine do scan work proportional to the bytes it allocated. That assist — not a monolithic pause — is what produces those small p99 wobbles under allocation pressure, and it is why the pacer’s heap goal (gcPercentHeapGoal, L149) matters for latency tuning. gcMarkDone, L997 closes the mark phase, and bgsweep, L285 reclaims spans lazily in the background. Note also that forcegcperiod, L6540 forces a cycle every two minutes even if the heap goal is never reached — a quiet source of periodic latency in allocation-light services.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository’s own README keeps it simple: official binary distributions are available at go.dev/dl/, with installation instructions linked from the docs, and for unsupported platform combinations the source-install instructions live at go.dev/doc/install/source. The canonical Git repository is hosted at go.googlesource.com/go, with github.com/golang/go acting as the read-only mirror this tour used. The Go source is distributed under a BSD-style license found in the repo’s LICENSE file.

From source to a running program, the toolchain is entirely self-hosted. The go command’s build path is implemented in src/cmd/go/internal/work — CmdBuild, L29 with runBuild at L465 — and each package is compiled by cmd/compile, whose Main, L67 wires inlining and escape analysis before the SSA backend takes over at buildssa, L302. The SSA pass table, from initial deadcode elimination through lower to lowered cse, is declared in compile.go, L414. The mental model to carry into your first concurrent program: the compiler emits the code, but the runtime you now understand decides when, where, and on which stack it runs.

Honest Limits

This tour is deliberately narrow. The scheduler code shown here is the mainstream path in proc.go; OS specifics leak through — extra stack headroom is added only on Windows and Plan 9 (stack.go, L75). The netpoller’s actual event loop is implemented per OS — epoll, kqueue, IOCP — outside the generic netpoll.go we touched, so its internals deserve a separate tour. Line numbers are pinned to the master tree as of this writing and will drift; the symbols, not the numbers, are the durable knowledge. And whole subsystems remain unopened: timer heaps (checkTimers), cgo transitions, the trace reader, and the pacer’s control theory in mgcpacer.go.
entry.summary: A verified source tour of the golang/go runtime showing how the G/M/P scheduler, channel blocking, tricolor garbage collector, and per-P memory allocator execute every goroutine you spawn.

entry.title: How Node.js Actually Runs Your Code: Bootstrap, the Event Loop, and the Thread Pool in the Source

link.title: How Node.js Actually Runs Your Code: Bootstrap, the Event Loop, and the Thread Pool in the Source

entry.content:
Every Node.js developer eventually meets the same wall: one synchronous call — a tight JSON parse, a CPU-bound transform, a blocking hash — and the whole server freezes. Requests queue, timers slip, health checks fail. The usual explanation, “JavaScript is single-threaded,” is true but useless; it doesn’t tell you what is actually stuck or why async code is the fix. The real answer lives in the C++ layer under your require().

The second mystery is the event loop. It gets drawn as a diagram with six colored boxes, as if it were a scheduler Node ships. It isn’t. It is one C function, uv_run, inside libuv — a library Node vendors into its own tree — and the phases people talk about are the literal statements of a while loop in that function. Once you read it, setTimeout vs setImmediate ordering, process.nextTick semantics, and why the process exits when handlers finish all stop being folklore.

The third puzzle is the thread pool. If JavaScript runs on one thread, who does the blocking? File reads, DNS-style lookups and similar work vanish into a small set of worker threads — four by default — managed by libuv, with their completions funneled back into the loop you already understand. This post tours the actual execution path in the nodejs/node repository on the main branch: every file, symbol, and line number below was grepped and verified against the real tree, not reconstructed from blog posts.

Overview: the five stages between your terminal and your code — C++ bootstrap, JS bootstrap, module loading, the libuv event loop, and the worker thread pool that absorbs blocking I/O.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The whole runtime is an embedded V8 program. On Unix, main, L96 is essentially return node::Start(argc, argv) — nothing else happens before it.
  • Start, L1848 delegates to StartInternal, L1776, which does process-global setup once: argument fixing, InitializeOncePerProcessInternal, L1783, and configuring the default loop with idle-time metrics at uv_loop_configure, L1806.
  • The per-process work ends by constructing a NodeMainInstance::Run, L89 over uv_default_loop(), which calls CreateMainEnvironment at L126 — deserializing a build-time startup snapshot, or making a fresh context.
  • JS core loads before any user code: LoadEnvironment, L597 triggers Realm::RunBootstrapping, L190, which executes internal/bootstrap/realm.js, home of the BuiltinModule, L245 registry that backs internalBinding().
  • Standard streams are wired by probing file descriptors: guessHandleType, L53 switches on TTY/FILE/PIPE/TCP to decide what stdout actually is.
  • One of the main scripts in lib/internal/main is selected by C++, and prepareMainThreadExecution, L49 applies run-time state (CLI options, argv expansion) before anything user-owned runs.
  • The entry point goes through the CommonJS loader’s public face first: run_main_module.js calls Module.runMain, which is aliased at L520 to executeUserEntryPoint, L146.
  • That loader decision is deliberate: unless shouldUseESMLoader, L53 says otherwise, the entry is attempted as CommonJS via wrapModuleLoad at L173, with an ESM retry path for ambiguous files.
  • After the entry runs, control never returns to the “end of script”: NodeMainInstance::Run spins SpinEventLoopInternal, L23, a do/while that alternates uv_run, L427 with NodePlatform::DrainTasks, L579 until the loop dies.

The detail view adds the binding layer, both module loaders, the timer round-trip between C++ and JS, the fs-to-threadpool path, and per-worker loops.

A Bootstrap You Can Trace in Two Files

The C++ side is remarkably linear. src/node_main.cc is a thin shell; src/node.cc holds the real sequence. StartInternal sets up process state once per process, then the interesting choice: CreateMainEnvironment, L126 either reads the context out of an embedded V8 startup snapshot or builds a new one. The snapshot is real — lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js documents at L7-L16 that its heap is captured by node_mksnapshot at build time, and passing --no-node-snapshot makes Node actually execute that script on each start.

Inside the realm bootstrap, lib/internal/bootstrap/realm.js installs the built-in module machinery and the internalBinding() bridge; lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js then sets up the global and process objects in a deliberately synchronous, environment-independent way. Only after that do the switches/ scripts run, wiring stdio based on what the descriptor turns out to be. This two-layer split explains a subtle fact: code in the bootstrap phase must not perform async operations, which is exactly why your first I/O doesn’t happen until lib/internal/main scripts take over.

The Binding Layer: How C++ Exposes Itself to JS

There is no magic require for native code at this level — there is a registry. GetInternalBinding, L997 hands JS the exports object of a compiled-in native module, and RegisterExternalReferences, L1083 is where each subsystem registers its callbacks with the V8 external-reference table so they can be fast-called.

Timers show the round-trip crisply. JS calls internalBinding('timers') (lib/internal/timers.js L85) and hands C++ two functions through SetupTimers (src/timers.cc). When a libuv timer expires, Environment::RunTimers, L1773 — started via uv_timer_start at L1760 — invokes the stored callback, which is JS’s processTimers, L596. Your setTimeout callback therefore enters your code from inside a C function that libuv scheduled; that is the entire “magic.”

The Event Loop Is a C Function with Seven Phases

Open uv_run, L427 and the diagram becomes code. After checking uv__loop_alive, a while loop at L445 runs: pending callbacks, idle handles, prepare handles, then uv__io_poll, L460 with a computed timeout, then check and closing handles, then uv__run_timers, L478. The “phases” are just these calls in order.

Node wraps this: SpinEventLoopInternal, L23 repeatedly calls uv_run and DrainTasks, L579 — which flushes V8 platform foreground tasks for the isolate (FlushForegroundTasksInternal, L607) — then checks uv_loop_alive and emits beforeExit for a last chance to keep living. The process exits when nothing alive remains: no open handles, no pending timers, no unsettled promises the loop cares about.

CommonJS or ESM: The Decision at Startup

For node entry.js, lib/internal/main/run_main_module.js ends with Module.runMain(mainEntry), which is aliased at L520 to executeUserEntryPoint — so even ESM entries enter through the CJS loader’s public surface, a compatibility choice documented in that file. shouldUseESMLoader, L53 checks extension and package type; when ESM wins, importForEntryPoint, L184 drives ESMLoader.import, L682, returning a promise only when top-level await is involved.

CommonJS loading itself is Module._load, L1341: a per-directory relative-resolve cache for fast repeats, a Module._cache hit path, circular-dependency handling that returns partial exports, and hook-aware resolution. The cache is why require is idempotent per file — and why a module that throws can leave a half-initialized entry behind.

The Thread Pool: Where Blocking Work Actually Goes

libuv keeps a small worker pool: default_threads, L39 has four entries, sized from UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE at L207, capped at 1024. Work is submitted through uv_queue_work, L379; completions wake the loop. Node’s file layer rides on this: every uv_fs_* operation executes in uv__fs_work, L1679 and is submitted via uv__work_submit, and src/node_file.cc dispatches async reads with uv_fs_read at L637.

Streams sit on top of these handles. Readable, L344 with Readable.prototype.read, L700 implements push/pull with backpressure buffers — the reason piping a large response doesn’t balloon memory. For concurrency beyond one isolate, worker_threads spawn real OS threads via uv_thread_create_ex, L781, and each worker runs its own SpinEventLoopInternal, L438. If you embed a synchronous local store like SQLite in-process, its speed profile is yours to manage — the pool will not absorb it for you.

From Install to Your First Model

Building Node from source is ordinary autotools-style work, fully documented in the repo. From a clone of nodejs/node, the canonical sequence is ./configure followed by make -j4 (BUILDING.md, L359-L360); expect roughly 8 GB of RAM when compiling with four parallel jobs (L243), and a g++ or clang compatible with C++20 (L366). make -j4 test runs the full check suite including documentation tests (L412).

The resulting ./node binary is everything above in one executable. Your first run — say a script that calls a hosted LLM endpoint or streams tokens to the console — exercises the exact path in this tour: main → StartInternal → snapshot deserialize → bootstrap realm → executeUserEntryPoint → uv_run. Node itself ships no model runtime; it is a JS host, so anything LLM-flavored arrives as npm dependencies, or as frameworks built on it like Express and Hono. The Python-minded can compare this whole bootstrap story with CPython, where the interpreter loop and GIL play the roles libuv and the isolate play here.

Honest Limits

  • One isolate, one loop. A synchronous call blocks its own isolate’s event loop — the fix spaces are: move work to the pool (libuv-managed only), to a worker thread, or to another process. The pool does not rescue unbounded JS computation; it only carries submitted libuv work such as the fs path shown above.
  • Pool defaults are small on purpose: four workers (L39), tunable via UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE up to 1024. A full audit of which Node subsystems use the pool versus dedicated threads was out of scope here — the fs path is verified end-to-end; crypto and DNS internals were not traced in this tour.
  • Bootstrap JS mostly doesn’t run at startup: it is deserialized from the build-time snapshot (L13), so profiling “cold start” with --no-node-snapshot measures a different program than production.
  • This tour follows the Unix execution path; libuv ships a parallel Windows implementation in deps/uv/src/win/core.c, and the phase machine there is a separate file. Ordering rules that developers feel — timers, immediates, next-ticks — also live partly in JS (lib/internal/timers.js) and partly in C++, so “one source of truth” for ordering claims doesn’t exist in a single file.
entry.summary: A verified walk through the nodejs/node tree — from int main() through V8 bootstrap, the binding layer, CommonJS/ESM loading, libuv's phase machine, and the 4-worker thread pool.
